label: anxious-preoccupied attachment
source_text: Preoccupied - I want to be completely emotionally intimate with others, but I often find that others are reluctant to get as close as I would like. I am uncomfortable being without close relationships, but I sometimes worry that others don't value me as much as I value them. [Model: negative self / positive partner; 'the preoccupied style of attachment is characterized by high anxiety and low avoidance'.]
description_draft: This means wanting complete emotional intimacy, often finding others reluctant to come as close, feeling uncomfortable without close relationships, and sometimes worrying that one values others more than they value one.
nearest_existing: clingy (the hanging-on behavior; this pole adds the wish for complete intimacy and the worry about not being valued back); also insecure, dependent, anxious.
notes: Hedges kept: 'often', 'sometimes'; 'completely' rendered as 'complete'. Source: Wikipedia, 'Attachment measures', section on Bartholomew and Horowitz, which reproduces the four 1991 prototype paragraphs verbatim under the names Secure / Dismissive / Preoccupied / Fearful and cites Bartholomew, K. & Horowitz, L. M. (1991), 'Attachment styles among young adults: a test of a four-category model', JPSP 61, 226-244. The paper itself is not openly hosted (PubMed 1920064 served only a cookie page; no open PDF found) and Bartholomew's SFU self-report page is a 404, so this reproduction stands in for it. The Wikipedia article 'Attachment in adults', which the packet names, no longer carries the paragraphs: its raw wikitext (fetched today) has only the sentence that its style descriptions are based on the RQ. Second source, the questionnaire as distributed: R. Chris Fraley's measures page (University of Illinois), https://labs.psychology.illinois.edu/~rcfraley/measures/rq.html, styles A-D with no names (psytests.org/ipl/rqen-bl.html has the identical text). The distributed RQ drops some of the paper's hedges: A reads 'It is easy for me' (paper: 'relatively easy'); B reads 'I am uncomfortable getting close' and 'I worry that I will be hurt' (paper: 'somewhat uncomfortable', 'I sometimes worry'). The draft keeps the paper's hedges, as the packet asks. Names: the paper uses secure / fearful / preoccupied / dismissing (so also Cozzarelli et al. 2003, UCSB Close Relationships Lab PDF); Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' uses Secure / Fearful / Preoccupied / Dismissive; the queue's labels are the hybrid names. The two axes: Wikipedia 'Attachment measures' maps model of self to attachment anxiety and model of partner to avoidance: secure low/low, preoccupied high anxiety/low avoidance, dismissive low anxiety/high avoidance, fearful high/high.
set_review: Attachment square. Avoidance (comfort with closeness and mutual dependence) comes through in all four: secure finds closeness relatively easy and depends comfortably; preoccupied wants complete intimacy and is uncomfortable without close relationships; dismissive is comfortable without them and prefers not to depend or be depended on; fearful is somewhat uncomfortable getting close and finds it hard to trust or depend. Anxiety (worry about being valued, accepted, hurt) comes through in three corners as stated worry or its absence: secure does not worry about being alone or unaccepted; preoccupied sometimes worries others value them less; fearful sometimes worries about being hurt. The dismissive corner carries low anxiety only by implication (self-sufficiency, no worry mentioned), exactly as the source prototype does, so the anxiety axis is readable from three corners and inferred for the fourth. The two worries differ in object (being valued less vs being hurt), so the axis is a shared theme, not a repeated word. Strength: the fearful corner is the mildest (two hedges, 'somewhat' and 'sometimes'), the dismissive the flattest (no hedge, 'very important'), mirroring the source; preoccupied carries 'often' and 'sometimes'; secure 'relatively'. All four are one grain (one's stance toward closeness and dependence in close relationships, plus the worry or its absence) and one shape (gerund triplets, 30-32 words).

label: conventional (Kohlberg)
source_text: 2. Conventional Level. At this level, maintaining the expectations of the individual's family, group or nation is perceived as valuable in its own right, regardless of immediate and obvious consequences. The attitude is not only one of conformity to personal expectations and social order, but of loyalty to it, of actively maintaining, supporting, and justifying the order and of identifying with the persons or group involved in it. [...] Stage 3. The Interpersonal Concordance or "Good Boy - Nice Girl" Orientation. Good behaviour is that which pleases or helps others and is approved by them. [...] "he means well" becomes important for the first time. Stage 4. The Law-and-Order Orientation. [...] Right behaviour consists of doing one's duty, showing respect for authority, and maintaining the given social order for its own sake.
description_draft: This means taking what one's family, group or country expects as right in itself, whatever follows: pleasing others and meaning well, doing one's duty, respecting authority and upholding the social order.
nearest_existing: conventional (plain; already in the corpus, so this is a deliberate standard's near-duplicate, to be said in `source`); conformist and rule_abiding are the behavioral neighbors; this pole is the basis of judgment: the group's expectations held as right in themselves, with loyalty to the order.
notes: 'Regardless of immediate and obvious consequences' rendered as 'whatever follows'; 'nation' as 'country'; 'frequently judged by intention' as 'meaning well'. No hedge in the level text to carry. Source: Marcus David Feak, 'Moral Development and its Explanation: Kohlberg's Structuralism', MA thesis (Philosophy), McMaster University, August 1979, pp. 3-5, which reproduces Kohlberg's chart 'Definition of Moral Stages' in full and cites it '(1972, 296-297)', i.e. Kohlberg, L., 'Relativity and Indoctrination in Value Education', Zygon 7 (Spring 1972), 285-309, per the thesis bibliography. Kohlberg's own publications of this chart (Zygon 1972; J. Phil. 1973, 630-646; Phi Delta Kappan 1975; Kohlberg & Hersh, Theory Into Practice 1977) are all paywalled, so a quoting scholarly source is used, as the packet allows. The thesis PDF is a scan; its OCR was cleaned for source_text (hyphenation joined; 'ac~!on' -> 'action', 'group pr nation' -> 'group or nation', 'persons or groups or group' -> 'persons or group', 'mora I v1tlues' -> 'moral values', 'tenTIS' -> 'terms', 'Le alistic' -> 'Legalistic', 'Oritntation' -> 'Orientation', 'respect 0 the dig-jljty' -> 'respect for the dignity'; the Stage 3 heading is illegible in the OCR and is supplied from the second reproduction). British spellings ('favours', 'behaviour') are the thesis's. Second reproduction, same chart with an extra Stage 0 and small wording differences ('the individual perceives the maintenance of the expectations of his family...', 'The individual makes a clear effort to define...'): https://xenodochy.org/ex/lists/moraldev.html (Ralph Kenyon, personal site, naming its source as Kohlberg's chapter in M. C. Reynolds (ed.), Psychology and the Process of Schooling in the Next Decade: Alternative Conceptions, c. 1971); a Prince Sultan University handout PDF has the same text. Scholarly paraphrase cross-check: W. C. Crain (1985), Theories of Development, ch. 7, HTML copy at https://www.appstate.edu/~steelekm/classes/psy2664/kohlberg.htm (its Kohlberg quotations are about stages, not levels). Not reachable: the Kohlberg 1976 passage on the three levels as 'three different types of relationships between the self and society's rules and expectations' (Hockenbury textbook table host unreachable; Sage Encyclopedia of Educational Theory and Philosophy paywalled; the SEP 'Moral Psychology: Empirical Approaches' entry does not discuss Kohlberg). Wikipedia 'Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development' paraphrases the levels (citing Kohlberg 1971, 1976 and Colby & Kohlberg 1987) and has no verbatim level text.
set_review: Kohlberg three. The descriptions read as a triangle rather than an ordered sequence. Each names a distinct basis for deciding right and wrong: what the act brings oneself and who has the power (pre), what one's group expects, held as right in itself (conv), principles worked out for oneself and valid apart from any group (post). Nothing in the three texts says earlier/later or less/more adequate, so the developmental order of the source is not readable from them; a reader meets three ways of judging, each contrastable with each other. The pairwise contrasts are all live: pre vs conv is self-interest and power against loyalty to the group; conv vs post is the group's authority against principles above the group; pre vs post is consequences-to-self against self-chosen principle. One caveat for the geometry: pre and post share a feature that a strict line would not predict, both set the group's expectations aside (one for payoff, one for principle), which is the confusion Kohlberg himself warned of between his lowest and highest stages, so the pre-post distance need not be the longest, and a sequence reading (conv in the middle) is not supported by the texts. Grain and shape are matched: each opens 'This means <gerund>' and states the basis of judgment, 30-31 words.

label: dismissive-avoidant attachment
source_text: Dismissive - I am comfortable without close emotional relationships. It is very important to me to feel independent and self-sufficient, and I prefer not to depend on others or have others depend on me. [Model: positive self / negative partner; 'the dismissive avoidant style of attachment is characterized by low anxiety and high avoidance'.]
description_draft: This means being comfortable without close emotional relationships, setting great store by feeling independent and self-sufficient, and preferring neither to depend on others nor to have them depend on oneself.
nearest_existing: self_reliant (doing things oneself; this pole is comfort without close relationships and a preference against mutual dependence); also detached, independent, avoidant, emotionally_disengaged.

label: fearful-avoidant attachment
source_text: Fearful - I am somewhat uncomfortable getting close to others. I want emotionally close relationships, but I find it difficult to trust others completely, or to depend on them. I sometimes worry that I will be hurt if I allow myself to become too close to others. [Model: negative self / negative partner; 'the fearful avoidant style of attachment is characterized by high anxiety and high avoidance'.]
description_draft: This means being somewhat uncomfortable getting close: wanting emotionally close relationships yet finding others hard to trust or depend on completely, and sometimes worrying about being hurt by letting anyone too close.
nearest_existing: guarded (withholding; this pole wants closeness and fears the hurt, the approach-avoid conflict); also avoidant, insecure, trusting's opposite side.
notes: Hedges kept: 'somewhat', 'sometimes'; 'completely' kept. This is the hedged 1991 wording; the distributed RQ reads 'I am uncomfortable getting close' and 'I worry that I will be hurt' (see below). The mildest of the four, as in the source. label: postconventional (Kohlberg)
source_text: 3. Postconventional, Autonomous, or Principled Level. At this level, there is a clear effort to define moral values and principles which have validity and application apart from the authority of the groups or persons holding these principles and apart from the individual's own identification with these groups. [...] Stage 5. The Social Contract Legalistic Orientation. [...] Right action tends to be defined in terms of general individual rights and in terms of standards which have been critically examined and agreed upon by the whole society. [...] Stage 6. The Universal Ethical Principle Orientation. Right is defined by the decision of conscience in accord with self-chosen ethical principles [...]. At heart, these are universal principles of justice [...] and of respect for the dignity of human beings as individual persons.
description_draft: This means working out for oneself the principles of rights and justice one judges by, and holding them valid apart from any group's authority and from one's loyalty to that group.
nearest_existing: principled (holds to principles; this pole is where the principles come from and that they stand above any group's authority); also moral_universalist, autonomy_respecting, deontological, utilitarian, nonconformist.
notes: 'Rights and justice' summarizes the two stages' content (individual rights and critically examined standards; universal principles of justice and human dignity); 'the individual's own identification with these groups' rendered as 'one's loyalty to that group'. The stage-5 hedge 'tends to be defined' is not carried because the level sentence, which the draft follows, has none. label: preconventional (Kohlberg)
source_text: 1. Preconventional Level. At this level the child is responsive to cultural rules and labels of good and bad, right or wrong, but interprets these labels in terms of either the physical or hedonistic consequences of action (punishment, reward, exchange of favours) or in terms of the physical power of those who enunciate the rules and labels. [...] Stage 1. The Punishment and Obedience Orientation. [...] Stage 2. The Instrumental Relativist Orientation. Right action consists of that which instrumentally satisfies one's own needs and occasionally the needs of others. Human relations are viewed in terms like those of the market place. [...] Reciprocity is a matter of "you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours", not of loyalty, gratitude or justice.
description_draft: This means judging an act right or wrong by what it brings oneself, whether punishment, reward or a favor returned, and by the power of whoever lays down the rule.
nearest_existing: expedient and transactional (self-interested conduct and dealing; this pole is a basis of moral judgment: right is what pays or what the powerful demand); also selfish, amoral, gain_seeking, obedient (deference to power).
notes: The source says 'the child'; the trait is any person reasoning this way, so the draft drops the age. 'Physical or hedonistic consequences (punishment, reward, exchange of favors)' rendered as 'what it brings oneself, whether punishment, reward or a favor returned'; 'the physical power of those who enunciate the rules' as 'the power of whoever lays down the rule'. No hedge in the level text. label: secure attachment
source_text: Secure - It is relatively easy for me to become emotionally close to others. I am comfortable depending on others and having others depend on me. I don't worry about being alone or having others not accept me. [Model: positive self / positive partner; 'The secure style of attachment is characterized by low anxiety and low avoidance'.]
description_draft: This means finding it relatively easy to get emotionally close to others, being comfortable depending on them and having them depend on oneself, and not worrying about being alone or unaccepted.
nearest_existing: trusting (trusts what people say; this pole is comfort with closeness and mutual dependence, and no worry about being left or unaccepted); also self_assured, happily_partnered (a status, not a style), emotionally_engaged.
notes: Hedge kept: 'relatively' (the distributed RQ drops it: 'It is easy for me').
